title: The Islands Kept Their Words — Teouma Lapita Ancient Genomes in Vanuatu, Near-Complete Papuan Ancestry Turnover & Why Austronesian Oceanic Languages Persisted

teenKit.tldr: When a 2003 bulldozer accidentally uncovered a 3,000-year-old cemetery in Vanuatu, it revealed that ancient islanders' DNA, pots, and languages didn't all travel together. This discovery rewrote how scientists track human migration across the Pacific.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It proves that human history isn't a straight line—our genes, cultures, and languages can completely decouple and evolve along totally separate tracks.
keyTakeaways: A routine quarry operation in 2003 unearths the Teouma site, a massive 3,000-year-old Lapita culture cemetery in Vanuatu.
The earliest people buried there carried minimal Papuan ancestry, showing that early Pacific voyagers were genetically distinct from later populations.
Even though later migrations completely replaced the local gene pool, the original Austronesian Oceanic languages miraculously stuck around.

vocab.meaning: An ancient seafaring culture known for expanding across Remote Oceania and leaving behind distinct, intricately stamped pottery.
A pottery-decorating technique where artists used comb-like tools to press geometric patterns into wet clay before firing.
A genetic shift where one population moves into an area and largely replaces the DNA of the existing population over time.
A massive language family spread across the Pacific islands by early maritime explorers.
